global.headline: Araghchi sets out Hormuz timetable as France deploys to Yanbu
summary: Abbas Araghchi set out the sequence: within four to five days Washington lifts the naval blockade, restores the oil-export waiver, ends the war on all fronts and releases frozen assets; on day six Iran reopens Hormuz via a route agreed with Oman; on day seven nuclear talks begin, pulled forward from June's 60 days.

What is new is the speed, not the terms, he said. He doubts Steve Witkoff can deliver, and Marco Rubio called Tuesday's meeting no breakthrough. Saudi Arabia intercepted six Houthi missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu; Macron is sending soldiers, radars and air defences to protect Yanbu; Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad called urgent chiefs-of-staff talks under their joint defence pact. Oil rose about 3%, then eased.
global.geopolitical: The route runs mainly through Iranian waters and was agreed bilaterally with Oman, not with the Gulf states as co-signatories — hence Riyadh's unhappiness. Trump's hardest condition is ordering Israel to stop in Lebanon, which Washington has not shown it will do.
global.socioeconomic: France is now underwriting the alternative Red Sea export route while the Hormuz one stays shut, and Pakistan is being drawn toward a war its officials do not want. Crude's retreat from session highs says the market prices the blockade, not the proposal.

global.headline: Tigray war resumes as Ethiopia restricts internet access
summary: Internet access was restricted across Tigray on Friday, two days after Tigrayan forces seized three federally held airports and fighting spread into Amhara and Afar. In the 2020–22 war the region was cut off entirely. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended all Tigray flights.

Tigray's government says federal troops attacked first; Getachew Reda, an adviser to Abiy Ahmed, says the TPLF launched an all-out offensive. ACLED dates the fighting to 1 August near the Sudanese border. The 2022 Pretoria Agreement ended a war estimated to have killed 600,000 people. “It was systematically hollowed out over three years,” researcher Surafel Getahun told CNN, faulting both sides.
global.geopolitical: An African Union-brokered settlement, the continent's showcase peace deal, has failed on its own terms, with former enemies now fighting side by side. Eritrea's absence from the agreement leaves the most dangerous actor with no obligations under it.
global.socioeconomic: A communications blackout is how the last war's famine went unrecorded for months, so restricting Tigray's internet removes the evidence base aid agencies work from. Separately, Aliko Dangote is helping fund a US$660m fuel pipeline from Djibouti into landlocked Ethiopia.

global.headline: US intelligence tells Congress Saudi Arabia has not ruled out a bomb
summary: Classified documents given to Congress include a US intelligence assessment that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, The Washington Post reported. They form part of the review of the civil nuclear agreement signed on 22 July by energy secretary Chris Wright and Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, and sent to Congress on 25 August.

The 30-year agreement caps enrichment below 5% but lets the ceiling rise to 20% after a further study and written agreement — most of the separative work needed to reach weapons-grade 90%. The State Department's input reads as more confident in the safeguards. Senators Markey, Merkley and Bennet want the two classified side letters released.
global.geopolitical: The assessment lands while Iran publicly refuses any ceiling on its own enrichment. A 20% Saudi ceiling would make the American case against Iranian enrichment impossible to state consistently, and Mohammed bin Salman has said since 2018 that Riyadh would follow Tehran.
global.socioeconomic: The deal's commercial point is American reactor vendors and a 30-year fuel relationship. Congress's default is passivity — the clock runs out and the agreement enters force — so the side letters nobody outside the committees has read carry the real terms.

global.headline: Zelensky says Trump has cleared Ukraine to build Patriot missiles
summary: “There are concrete agreements in place,” Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters, quoting Trump at their UN meeting: “I have made the final decision: Ukraine will receive a license to manufacture Patriot missiles.” Trump floated this at July's Nato summit in Turkey and cooled on it weeks later; the White House has not commented.

Zelensky said in August that Ukraine holds about a tenth of the interceptors it needs. On Friday seven civilians, including a teenager, were killed and 59 injured in daytime drone strikes on Kyiv, one of eight regions hit. Washington has proposed trilateral talks with Russia in the UAE, with no date set.
global.geopolitical: A production licence, not a delivery, is the change: it moves Ukraine from queuing behind other buyers to making its own interceptors, and it is much harder for a future administration to switch off than a shipment.
global.socioeconomic: Licensed Patriot production would put high-end defence manufacturing inside a country whose industry is itself the target of the strikes. It also eases the interceptor shortage that has had dozens of governments bidding against each other.

global.headline: Supreme Court clears citizenship database for voter checks
summary: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on Friday that states may use the Department of Homeland Security's revamped SAVE system — Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements — to check voters' citizenship, lifting Judge Sparkle Sooknanan's June order that the overhaul breached federal privacy law.

The unsigned majority held that Washington “has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials”, stressed individualised checks, and noted the ban on systematic purges within 90 days of an election; the administration says that ban excludes non-citizen purges, a question the court will hear separately. DHS concedes SAVE's results are not always accurate. Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented with Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan.
global.geopolitical: A 1980s benefits-eligibility database is now election infrastructure, weeks before the midterms, decided on an emergency docket without full argument. The reasoning — a federal duty to answer states overriding privacy limits — travels to any federal dataset.
global.socioeconomic: The cost of a false match falls on the voter, who must prove citizenship to stay registered. DHS conditioned anti-terrorism grants on states adopting SAVE for audits, pushing the administrative burden onto state election offices.

singapore.headline: Singapore crosses into super-aged society at 21.4%
summary: Population in Brief 2026, published by the National Population and Talent Division on 25 September, puts 21.4% of citizens at 65 or older — past the UN's 21% super-aged threshold, up from 20.7% last year and 13.7% a decade ago. Citizens aged 80 and above reached 152,000, a 60% rise in ten years.

The working-age share, 20 to 64, fell to 59.3% from 64.3% in 2016, and the ratio of working-age to elderly residents fell from 5.4 to 3.2. Total population rose 1.6% to 6.21 million, with non-residents contributing 70,300 of the 97,300 increase — driven by construction workers for Changi T5 and housing supply. Citizens rose 0.7% to 3.68 million.
singapore.geopolitical: A shrinking working-age base makes the immigration numbers structural rather than discretionary, which narrows the room any government has to answer public pressure on the size of the foreign workforce.
singapore.socioeconomic: 3.2 working-age residents per elderly resident is the figure that sets healthcare and CPF arithmetic for the next decade. Sociologists warned ST that over-65s becoming a larger share of the electorate risks zero-sum intergenerational politics; nearly one in three residents over 65 was already working in 2025.

singapore.headline: PSD to review rail planners' property purchases from 2007 to 2011
summary: The Public Service Division said on 25 September it is identifying and reviewing home purchases made between 2007 and 2011 by officers involved in rail planning, where properties were close to sites later announced as MRT stations. Evidence that an officer used non-public information for personal benefit will go to the police.

The review follows a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper finding that civil servants, particularly rail planners, disproportionately bought homes near stations not yet announced — a pattern that largely disappeared after 2011. PSD called the patterns “a concern” but said statistics alone do not establish that any officer had access to non-public information. Officers have had to declare property purchases since 1996.
singapore.geopolitical: A US academic paper, not an internal control, surfaced this — the uncomfortable part for a public service whose reputation for integrity is both a national asset and a selling point to investors.
singapore.socioeconomic: Records from 2007 to 2011 will be slow to retrieve and hard to read, so the practical outcome may be tightened declaration rules rather than individual findings. The 1996 declaration regime is the safeguard now on trial.

singapore.headline: HDB reviews jumbo flat scheme after $2.18m Telok Blangah listing
summary: The Housing Board is reviewing the scheme that lets owners combine three-room or smaller flats into a jumbo unit, after a 1,465 sq ft combined flat at 93B Telok Blangah Street 31 was listed at S$2.18 million.

HDB called the price “significantly higher” than comparable deals: three-room flats there have transacted between about S$673,000 and S$771,000 over six months, so two at the top of that range come to roughly S$1.54 million. The listing is more than S$600,000, or over 40%, above that — payable as cash over valuation, in full, up front. No resale application has been received; the scheme dates to 1993.
singapore.geopolitical: Nothing external, beyond the signal to overseas buyers watching whether Singapore's public housing stays rationed by policy rather than by price.
singapore.socioeconomic: The cash-over-valuation requirement is the real cap: a buyer needs over S$600,000 in cash that no loan or grant covers. Reviewing the 1993 scheme puts the route itself in question, not just this listing, near the Greater Southern Waterfront.

singapore.headline: Court lets 194,000 Jetstar Asia customers claim refunds without filing
summary: Written grounds issued on 24 September by the Singapore International Commercial Court explain why about 194,000 Jetstar Asia customers holding unused bookings and vouchers are entitled to S$11.4 million without proving their claims. International Judge Christopher Sontchi approved the restructuring scheme on 21 May.

All consumer creditors were placed in one “administrative convenience class”: excluded from voting, deemed to have unanimously approved the scheme, and not required to file a proof of debt. Nearly 146,000 held vouchers worth under S$20. Sontchi set out when the mechanism may be used under Singapore law, and found no creditor adversely affected. Qantas funded the refunds.
singapore.geopolitical: A precedent that matters to Singapore's pitch as a restructuring venue: the SICC has now written down how mass consumer creditors can be handled, the practical obstacle in any airline or retail insolvency.
singapore.socioeconomic: Refunds reach customers who would never have filed paperwork for a S$20 voucher — the class exists because the cost of process exceeded the claims. It works only because a solvent parent funded it; an insolvent collapse would distribute nothing this way.

singapore.headline: Singapore and Japan sign two environment pacts in 60th anniversary year
summary: Grace Fu and Japan's environment minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa signed an upgraded Memorandum of Cooperation on Environmental Matters on 24 September, adding management of emerging contaminants and ground pollution removal to existing work on decarbonisation, air quality, waste, noise and water.

On 25 September Fu signed a renewed Memorandum of Cooperation on Climate Science and Climate Adaptation with transport minister Tatsunori Ibayashi, covering coastal protection, flood resilience, stormwater management and weather services. Fu said the pacts advance cooperation “as we navigate geopolitical uncertainty” and pointed to Singapore's 2027 ASEAN chairmanship. Nearly 40 water-sector representatives began a Japan study trip on 25 September, visiting Tokyo Bay and Sendai sea defences.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is stacking bilateral technical agreements ahead of its 2027 ASEAN chairmanship, with a partner that has no stake in the US-China contest over standards. Anniversaries produce signings; the coastal protection content is the substantive part.
singapore.socioeconomic: Japan has spent decades and very large sums on the sea defences Singapore is only starting to cost, and Sendai and Minamisanriku are the places that have rebuilt after the worst case. Early warning and meteorology cooperation is far cheaper than the concrete.

word.definition: The state of disuse into which a law or agreement falls when left unenforced.
word.etymology: From Latin desuetudo, from desuescere “to become unaccustomed” (de- “away” + suescere “be used to”); into English via French in the 1600s.
word.example: Three years of desuetude emptied the Pretoria Agreement before Tigrayan forces seized the airports.
